title: POC scoping - latency SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT) - Pioneer Robotics
summary: AE+SE aligned with Pioneer on POC success criteria: define TTFT and TPOT SLOs (p95/p99), agree on workload sizing (QPS, concurrency, seq len), run two-phase benchmark (synthetic loadgen + e2e production-like tests), and deliver benchmark spec and pricing. Next: Redwood to send benchmark template, security docs, and proposed pilot timeline.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Pioneer CTO), Liam Chen (Head of Platform), Diane Park (SRE)

[00:00] Alex Monroe: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um i'll kick off quick agenda, we want to scope the poc for latency slos, specifically ttft vs tpot targets, verify workload sizing and agree benchmark plan and timeline
[00:14] Priya Nair: thanks alex, yeah we're particularly sensitive to first token latency for interactive agent flows, but also cost per token matters for batch inference; we want both TTFT and TPOT to be solid
[00:26] Samir Patel: hi all, i'm samir, i'll focus on the technical measurements and the load profiles, quick question first - what's your expected peak qps and concurrency for the pilot?
[00:38] Liam Chen: good question - for the pilot we want to simulate our end-of-day load and some steady-state interactive traffic. target peak qps ~150, sustained 60 qps, typical concurrency 20-30, but burst to 80 for short periods
[00:52] Diane Park: sequence lengths vary - chat messages avg 120 tokens, some longer multi-turn context up to 1k tokens but rare, and generation output is usually 30-80 tokens
[01:05] Priya Nair: to add, the user-facing SLA is 300ms p95 TTFT for short prompts (<=128 tokens), and 500ms p95 for medium prompts (~512 tokens). p99 we want <600ms for short prompts, <900ms for medium. those are our internal goals, can we validate?
[01:26] Samir Patel: okay that's helpful, just to align on definitions: when we say TTFT here we mean time-to-first-token from request received by the inference endpoint to first byte of generated token at client - including network hop within the deployment boundary but excluding client-side render. TPOT we define as time-per-output-token averaged over generation, often measured as throughput (tokens/sec) or per-token latency; some teams also look at tokens-per-second (tps) at the model runtime. does that match your definitions?
[01:47] Priya Nair: yes, that matches. we just want the end-to-end observable from our app to Redwood and back - we will instrument on our side too
[01:55] Alex Monroe: great. a few practical notes: for Hosted API we can usually meet those p95 numbers for short prompts, depending on model. Dedicated or private gives more headroom for p99 and for consistent burst performance. during the poc we should test both a hosted baseline and a dedicated configuration, if you can provide expected concurrency and token mix we can size the reserved capacity proposal
[02:18] Liam Chen: interested in both - baseline hosted to compare cost, then dedicated for production. what's the typical batch size / batching behavior that would affect TTFT?
[02:28] Samir Patel: batching is a big factor. continuous batching helps amortize cost and improve TPOT, but increases TTFT slightly when waiting to fill a batch. our runtime has dynamic batching with max batch wait thresholds; we'll instrument internal queuing time. for the measurement plan we'll capture queue time, kernel compute time, kv cache hits, and network serialization time.
[02:48] Diane Park: we also need KV cache behavior documented - some of our calls hit cached prefixes heavily which reduces compute and improves TTFT, but we'll want to see both cache-hit and cold-run numbers.
[02:59] Samir Patel: absolutely, we'll run three cache modes: cold (no cache), warm (populate with your prefix set), and steady-state typical hit-rate (you can provide sample traffic to approximate hit rates)
[03:12] Priya Nair: ok on success criteria: we have functional acceptance (correct outputs), performance acceptance (meet TTFT p95/p99 and TPOT thresholds), and reliability (99.9% availability during run). timelinewise, we want a 3-week pilot with benchmarks in week 2 and results in week 3
[03:28] Alex Monroe: 3-week pilot is reasonable. here's a proposed milestone breakdown: week 0 - kickoff and traffic/sample collection; week 1 - deploy dedicated/pilot env and sanity checks; week 2 - run synthetic and e2e benchmarks across models and quantization profiles; week 3 - analyze results and handoff decisions. does that map?
[03:46] Liam Chen: yes but we may need extra time for compliance review before dedicated provision - maybe +1 week if needed
[03:52] Alex Monroe: noted, we can run hosted benchmarks in parallel while compliance is reviewed
[03:57] [04:00] Priya Nair: technical question - how will you measure p95/p99? where will percentiles be computed (client-side vs server-side)
[04:07] Samir Patel: good point. we'll capture both: client-side observability (you measure end-to-end including network from your app) and server-side logs/metrics. percentile reporting will be computed on both datasets; discrepancies are analyzed (usually network variability causes higher client-side p99). we'll provide raw traces and aggregated percentiles for TTFT and TPOT.
[04:23] Diane Park: can you define TPOT reporting? we want p95/p99 for per-token latency and also tokens/sec for throughput curves at different concurrencies
[04:33] Samir Patel: we'll report: average tokens/sec at each concurrency level, per-token latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), and end-to-end per-request token throughput. Also will include time breakdown: queue time, model compute time, serialization, and network.
[04:46] Liam Chen: for benchmark models we're evaluating both an open Llama-like medium model and a smaller faster quantized 8-bit model. are both supported in your runtime?
[04:56] Samir Patel: yes, we support a variety of quantization profiles. in the POC we'll run: baseline full-precision model, int8 quantized variant, and a distilled smaller model. we'll include memory and cost estimates for each.
[05:12] Priya Nair: what about measuring tail latency under burst - we want to see p99 during 1-minute bursts to 80 qps
[05:20] Samir Patel: we'll include stress bursts in the load plan: 1-minute and 5-minute bursts and measure rolling p95/p99. also apply cold-start scenarios - node restarts and cache flushes - to validate graceful degradation and fallbacks.
[05:35] Alex Monroe: i'm hearing a few hard numbers to include in the benchmark spec: short prompt thresholds <=128 tokens with p95 <=300ms p99 <=600ms; medium ~512 tokens p95 <=500ms p99 <=900ms; target throughput sustained 60 qps and peak 150 qps, burst to 80 concurrency. does that capture it?
[05:52] Priya Nair: yes that's exactly what we want to see validated
[05:55] Liam Chen: also include a cost per 1M tokens estimate for each model variant, and per-hour reserved cost for dedicated pool so we can do TCO comparison
[06:04] Alex Monroe: yes we'll include cost modeling and a simple dashboard showing tokens/sec vs $/1k tokens tradeoff across profiles
[06:12] Diane Park: security - please send SOC2 and network architecture for private deployment, we need details on KMS, audit logs, and VPC peering options
[06:21] Alex Monroe: we'll attach the security pack and our network reference architecture. for private we support customer-managed KMS and audit log forwarding
[06:29] Samir Patel: measurement plan details: 1) baseline synthetic loadgen using wrk-style driver that issues requests with your token distribution; 2) e2e test where your app calls through our API to replicate real client-side latency; 3) kernel-level profiles captured on the node (compute time per layer) for deeper perf work; 4) repeat tests for cold/warm/steady-state cache scenarios. we'll supply the load scripts and runner specs
[06:53] Priya Nair: who will run the e2e tests - your team or ours? we prefer to run from our region to include network effects
[07:00] Samir Patel: we'll coordinate - Redwood can run hosted tests from our infra, and you run e2e from your environment. for dedicated we'll provide load driver config and assistance running in your VPC if needed
[07:12] Liam Chen: instrumentation - will you provide spans/traces so we can link requests between our app and the Redwood backend?
[07:18] Samir Patel: yes, we'll emit trace ids in response headers and provide a tracing hook. we can also share per-request IDs for troubleshooting
[07:26] Priya Nair: what's the plan for aggregating percentiles? sliding window? one-off sample windows? how do we avoid percentile misinterpretation for small sample sizes
[07:34] Samir Patel: we'll use a combined approach: per-run percentiles for each test window (e.g., 5-minute window) and aggregated percentiles across runs with sample-size weighting. we'll include raw distributions so you can compute your own percentiles if desired
[07:46] Alex Monroe: ok next steps recap - redwood to send benchmark template, load profile, security docs, and estimated cost worksheet; pioneer to provide sample traffic, target key prompt set, and preferred pilot nodes/region. schedule: aim to start in 1 week if samples available
[08:02] Priya Nair: sounds good, we'll try to share sample traffic by end of week and confirm compliance timeline by monday
[08:10] Diane Park: action item for me to scrub logs and provide typical token distribution and cache-hit rates
[08:16] Liam Chen: i'll follow up on procurement questions and whether we need a pilot contract
[08:21] Samir Patel: we'll also add a technical appendix to the benchmark spec that explains measurement definitions (TTFT = server receive -> first token out, TPOT = per-token latency and tokens/sec), and include example curl/SDK commands to measure both
[08:37] Priya Nair: one small ask - please include p99 on the client side for a 95th percentile confidence interval or some stability metric, we care about repeatability across runs
[08:46] Samir Patel: we can include bootstrapped confidence intervals and multi-run comparisons in the report
[08:52] Alex Monroe: great. any final questions?
[08:55] Priya Nair: none from me, thanks everyone
[08:57] Liam Chen: all good
[08:58] Diane Park: thanks
[09:00] Alex Monroe: thanks - we'll follow up with the doc set and proposed timeline

Transcript notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings (e.g., tpot sometimes transcribed as t-p-o-t, KV cache spelled as 'kay-vee' in quick talk). speaker labels approximate, filler words and overlaps present.
